en: Go into the earth with your herds.
Take heed, Jakyp, hear my words;
Saying ‘My son turned out wild,’
Can you begrudge him your herds?
You are ill-disposed;
Jakyp, can one rightly call you human?
Begrudging your wild son livestock,
You are a man without ancestry;
Ah, you are a man who lives for herds!
The towering dark hills,
Where is the dark valley, where the mountain pass?
Was it livestock you sought?
Take heed, Jakyp, hear my words;
Where are the Argyn and Kyrgyz people?
Will your herds stand beside you?
Grieving ‘The livestock is gone,’
Can one rightly call you human?
Yesterday, when your father Karakan died,
The treasury of Karakan,
The Black Kalmyk and Manchu peoples,
Beating us with resounding blows,
Divided it by the measure of a whip.
When they showed unheard-of fury,
When they searched every bundle,
When they slaughtered whoever looked back,
When they smashed the white palace,
When the Black Kalmyks entered,
Whoever spoke back,
They seized and battered,
Slit his very scalp.
The stubborn man who stood defiant,
They hung him by his elbows.
Whoever spoke back,
They seized and had him beaten,
Cut leather strips from his back.
Understand it fully, rich Jakyp:
That was when we died.
The humiliation of these Chinese,
We suffered it exactly two thousand times!
When they used all their strength,
When they tore children away,
All our hands tied behind our backs,
Driven away in humiliation,
We walked without turning, grieving.
Beyond your herds, rich Jakyp,
We were parted from our brothers.
One of us they drove away,
Think of it, hey, Jakyp,
To a mountain pass no person could reach;
One of us they drove away
To the land where the sun rises.
The Black Kalmyks used their might,
Slaughtered all our people.
Raiding the hills, they took the herds;
Invading the village, they took lives.
Yesterday, when the Chinese worked their wonders,
Destroyed the multitude,
And did as they pleased with us,
They took our women and girls as booty,
Made them slave women who carried out ashes.
The boys, young and older,
They made slaves to tend the cattle.
Think of it, hey, Jakyp:
Who did such things?
One of us went to Iren;
One of us they cast
Into a depth from which none returns.
You came to Altay driven into exile,
Lamenting, unable to find a way.
When you came to this Altay,
You sowed grain and dug ore,
Did many kinds of arduous work,
Gathered a san of cattle and raised herds.
‘My son turned out wild,’ you say;
Has God struck you?
These herds you grieve over,
Will they last until Judgment Day?!
This is what I say; know it truly.
Ah, Jakyp, blessed man,
Go into the earth with those horses!
Wild ewes and rams belong to the mountain;
These herds you grieve over,
If an enemy grows strong, one day they are his.
This wild child of yours will mend;
If he lives, one day he belongs to the people.
The wretched herds you gathered in vain,
When disaster cries out, one day they are its prey.
Were you not living, rich Jakyp,
With many herds and no child?
‘My son turned out wild,’ you say;
I see there is no miser like you!”
Trampling a patch of ground like a terrace,
Khan Baltay stood grieving,
Reproaching rich Jakyp:
“Rich Jakyp, let us settle on Altay's steppe.
Let us offer ourselves
For the wild child named Manas.
Let us hang an amulet about his neck.
He will be a son who ends your sorrow;
Let us raise this child.
Look, Jakyp, heed my words:
He is our companion, he our strength.
The hostile Black Chinese,
He is the son who will defeat them for us.
If he lives, you will see:
He will drive white deer as cattle.
If this Manas grows,
He will bring the whole world to submission.
If your warrior son grows,
Will any mortal dare face him?
Will an enemy approach him head-on?
Can a person make him bow?
Can whoever meets him remain alive?
Babbling so many words,
You stand inviting ill fortune.
Instead, rich Jakyp,
The six san of horses on the hills,
Let us drive and gather them.
All those vast herds,
Let us run them past in a line.
One that will not grow lean if ridden six months,
Until it reaches sixty asyy,
Whose teeth will not jut with age,
Let us find the finest horse.
These accursed herds,
Rather than keep them, let us slaughter them.
The six san of horses on the hills,
Let us gather them all.
All those horses,
Let us run them past in a line.
One that does not panic at a battle cry,
When a moonless night comes,
One that never takes a false step,
A karabayyr, a battle steed,
With sieve-like lungs and copper forelegs,
Let us find a swift horse.
Without letting a single person know,
Without letting anyone sense it,
Dress him in a coat no bullet can pierce,
Mount him on a horse no bullet can catch.
Where no person passes and no people know,
Among the Black Kalmyks and Manchus,
Without letting one of them know,
Without letting one of them sense it,
Let us keep Manas safe and raise him in the mountains.
When he grows to manhood and becomes a warrior,
When he becomes the equal of other men's sons,
Teaching him what he does not know,
Let us set him on his path thus.
Making him understand what he does not grasp,
Let us set him on the right path.
When we climb upward, let Manas
Be the support we lean upon.
When we descend, let Manas
Be the prop that holds us up.
This wild Manas,
Let the forty Kyrgyz households gather
And cherish him.
If the Black Kalmyks go mad,
For this child Manas,
When death comes, let us die!”
The words Akbaltay spoke,
The forty Kyrgyz households deemed right.
Making known what was unknown,
Akbaltay was learned indeed;
Making clear what was not understood,
Akbaltay was a goshawk indeed.
Wiser than the cunning,
Your dear elder Baltay,
Crying out like a white falcon,
His white beard shining,
Whetted his dark tongue.
“Do not tell people he is Manas!”
Dear Baltay poured forth his words.
At that time was bestowed
Manas's name Chong Jindi.
That Manas would become Manas,
What Black Kalmyk knew?
Suffering on Manas's account,
Rich Jakyp was consumed with worry.
When he saw Manas's bearing:
“He will utterly ruin me,” he said.
“Because of this child's ill-starred hour,
They will level my very stump,
Slaughter us all,” he said.
Rich Jakyp grieved.
Jakyp went and wept,
Tormented his senior wife:
“Hey, my senior wife Chyyyrdy,
God Most High, the Almighty,
Has indeed given us a child.
Chong Jindi, who pisses in water,
He has given us an unfinished one!
Gather the herds from pasture, wife;
Restrain this child of yours, wife!
Unless you restrain this child,
If he brings trouble upon the Kalmyks,
The Chinese are an ilek, we are alone.
If we fall to fighting the Chinese,
They will capture us alive,
They will put us in their dungeon!
Let your wild child not do this,
Lest these Kalmyks fall upon us
And search through a bundle.
Your son has turned out wild and unruly;
This child's wildness
Has no equal in the world.
The children of forty Kyrgyz households
He gathered and began a game.
Of the Black Kalmyks and Manchus,
Exactly twelve children
He utterly destroyed.
Not knowing, your Black Kalmyks
Blamed one another.
I heard word from those who came:
‘The Black Kalmyks and Manchus
Quarreled and bickered,
And there was slaughter,’ I heard.
‘They took poles from the ground,
Mounted stallions from the tethering line,
Seized one another by the collar and fought;
There was a terrible battle,’ they say.
‘Mares were raided and men died;
There was dreadful havoc,’ they say.
My senior wife, your son will not let us prosper.
If this Manas goes on like this,
He will surely not leave us safe!
Lamenting ‘We have no child,’
We have asked for a calamity.
We came to Altay driven into exile,
Wandering, unable to find a way;
We asked for a child.
We thought a child, but a wretch:
We have fallen into miserable trouble.
Unless he ceases this wildness,
If the Black Kalmyk people learn,
They will fall upon our heads,
Scatter all four kinds of livestock.
They will raid the mares in clouds of dust;
If we come near, these Kalmyks
Will punch our brains out everywhere.
They will bring forth, I fear,
Their long-distant grudges.
This son of yours has grown wild;
Will the Kalmyks not see his wildness?
Will they not call us wandering Burut?
There is no way to spur against them.
The great herds we have gathered,
Will they not devour them, leaving none?
The Kyrgyz living here,
Will they not flee, unable to find a way?
This san of cattle we have gathered,
Leaving not a yearling among the shod,
Will the Kalmyks not scatter it all?
Defiant, this wild son of yours
Does stubborn deeds against the Kalmyks,
